## Notation and Parameters

The normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution. Very few concepts in real life are truly normally distributed, but many are _approximately_ normal. The normal is also the limiting distribution for many common statistics and distributions, such as the binomial distribution when $n \rightarrow \infty$.

$$X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$$

$x$ = {-$\infty$ to +$\infty$} = *the sample space*  

$\mu$ = the mean of the distribution (expected value)

$\sigma^2$ = the variance of the distribution  

The **standard normal** distribution $Z$ has $\mu$ = 0 and $\sigma^2$ = $\sigma$ = 1.


## Alternative Notation

In probability theory, we tend to discuss the expected value and variance of random variables, and this is echoed in the common shorthand notation for the normal model, $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

Standard deviation is the square root of variance, $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$.

For the normal distribution, standard deviation is connected to certain properties of the curve. Among other things, the values $\mu \pm \sigma$ are the inflection points where the concavity of the curve changes from being concave down to concave up.

<hr>

[The IMS2E textbook](https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-mathematical#normal-distribution-model) and `R` use $\sigma$ rather than $\sigma^2$ in their normal curve notation, using the shorthand notation $N(\mu,\sigma)$. 

*In a new source or text, always check what notation they are using!*


## Probability Density Function (pdf)

Unlike the pmfs in discrete distributions, the probability density function (pdf) of a continuous distribution does not compute a probability, because the area under a point is zero. Instead, the pdf tells us the height of the function (y) at x. Below is the pdf of the normal distribution. 

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$$

The shape is a "bell curve". The critical parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ will determine the location, height, and width. The area beneath a normal distribution is always 1.

The mean can be any real number, and the standard deviation can be any positive real number. 


## Standard Normal Density Function

Again, the standard normal distribution has $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$. This simplifies the normal pdf expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \\[0.75em]
f(x) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\times1}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-0}{1}\right)^2} \\[0.75em]
f(x) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^2} \\[0.75em]
\end{aligned}
$$

It is symmetric around $x = 0$, with height = $1/\sqrt{2\pi} = 0.3989$.

## Visualizing the Standard Normal

```{r, fig.height = 4.25}
sn_pdf <- ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(0, 1)
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#707070"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-4, 4),
    breaks = seq(from = -4, to = 4, by = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Normal Distribution N(0, 1)",
    x = "x",
    y = "f(x)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
sn_pdf
```

Notice that there is very little area under the curve outside ± $3$.


## Another Normal Distribution

```{r, fig.height = 4.25}
mu <- 69
sigma <- 3
ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mu, sigma)
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#707070"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(mu - (4 * sigma), mu + (4 * sigma)),
    breaks = seq(mu - (4 * sigma), mu + (4 * sigma), sigma)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "US Adult Male Heights ~ N(μ = 69, σ = 9)",
    x = "inches",
    y = "f(x)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  annotate("label",
    x = 69,
    y = 0.05,
    label = "same area"
  ) +
  annotate("label",
    x = 62.0,
    y = 0.10,
    label = "different scaling"
  ) +
  geom_segment(aes(
    x = c(59.5, 63),
    xend = c(57, 66),
    y = c(0.10, 0.0925),
    yend = c(0.10, 0.001)
  ),
  arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm")),
  color = "#FE6100", size = 1.25
  )
```

Notice that there is very little area under the curve outside ± $3\sigma$.


## The Empirical Rule

```{r, fig.height = 2.25}
sn_pdf <- ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(0, 1)
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#707070"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-4, 4),
    breaks = seq(from = -4, to = 4, by = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Normal Distribution N(0, 1)",
    x = "x",
    y = "f(x)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
sn_pdf +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = seq(-3, 3, 1),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1.25,
    color = c("#785EF0", "#DC267F", "#FE6100", "black", "#FE6100", "#DC267F", "#785EF0")
  )
```

* approximately <span style="color: #FE6100;">$68\%$</span> of the curve's area is between $\mu \pm 1\sigma$ 
* approximately <span style="color: #DC267F;">$95\%$</span> of the curve's area is between $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ 
* approximately <span style="color: #785EF0;">$99.7\%$</span> of the curve's area is between $\mu \pm 3\sigma$ 

The tails extend to $\pm \infty$ ; any value of $x$ is *theoretically* possible. In any given problem context, there will be limits on the values.


## Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)

The probability of the random variable $X$ taking on a value less than or equal to a specific value $x$ is found using the CDF, which integrates the area under the curve. This is similar to summing a discrete distribution like the binomial or calculating an empirical cumulative distribution function for a sample of data. 

$$F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int\limits_{-\infty}^{x}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}dx$$

The normal distribution has no closed-form solution for $F(x)$. `R` has a function for the normal CDF (and its inverse, which we will discuss later). Prior to digital technology, people used [tables of solutions](http://www.z-table.com/) computed for the standard normal curve Z.


## Visualizing the Standard Normal

```{r, fig.height = 4.25}
sn_cdf <- ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = pnorm,
    args = list(0, 1)
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#707070"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-4, 4),
    breaks = seq(from = -4, to = 4, by = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Normal Distribution N(0, 1)",
    x = "x",
    y = "F(x)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
sn_cdf
```

Notice the logistic (S) shape with the inflection point at $\mu = 0$.

##

In other words, solving is the equivalent of integrating between 0 and 1 using the standard normal CDF with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$.

$$P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = \int\limits_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}dx = \int\limits_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^2}dx$$

$$0.8413477 - 0.5 = 0.3413477$$

## More on Quantiles

The quantiles are the cumulative percentages and percentiles labeled on the image below. Note the cumulative percentages associated with the Empirical Rule ($1\sigma$, $2\sigma$, and $3\sigma$ above and below $\mu$). These are true for all normal distributions.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/normaldist.jpg", dpi = 75)
```


## But what about $P(X = x)?$

The normal distribution is a continuous function, so the area under a point is zero and $P(X = x)$ is technically zero.

Many variables are theoretically continuous, but measurements are always inherently discrete---we round all our measurements to some number of decimal places. 

We treat $P(X = x)$ as a narrow area beneath the curve rather than a single point. For example, if I measure people's height in inches and round to two decimal places, the probability that a person is 70.00 inches tall (5'10") is modeled as the probability that they are between 69.995 and 70.005 inches.

We *never* use the pmf to compute probabilities; it only maps the function, with $f(x)$ = the height of the curve at $x$.


## Expected Value and Variance

The theoretical expected value and variance for any distribution are generally found as follows. We cannot integrate $f(x)$, but it can be demonstrated that [expected value](https://statproofbook.github.io/P/norm-mean) and [variance](https://statproofbook.github.io/P/norm-var) simplify to the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ for the normal distribution.

$$E[X] = \int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x f(x) \rightarrow \mu$$

$$Var[X] = \int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty} (x - \mu)^2 f(x) \rightarrow \sigma^2$$
